items.stem: In samples of size 5 from a U[0, 1] population, the mean of the distribution of the median is:
items.explanation: The median of five observations is X₍₃₎, and E(X₍ᵣ₎) = r/(n+1) = 3/6 = 1/2. Equivalently X₍₃₎ ~ Beta(3,3), whose mean is 3/(3+3). Quicker still: U[0,1] is symmetric about 1/2, so its sample median has expectation 1/2 for every n. This is June 2026 Q13.
items.check: Option D, 1, is the population's upper limit, not a mean. Any answer outside (0,1) or at an endpoint should be rejected immediately.

items.stem: For a sample of size n from U(0, 1), the rᵗʰ order statistic follows:
items.explanation: Substituting F(x) = x and f(x) = 1 into the general density gives [n!/((r−1)!(n−r)!)] x^(r−1)(1−x)^(n−r), which is exactly the Beta(r, n−r+1) density. Note the parameters sum to n + 1, which is what makes the mean r/(n+1). Option A reverses them, giving the distribution of X₍ₙ₋ᵣ₊₁₎.

items.stem: The cdf of the largest order statistic X₍ₙ₎ is:
items.explanation: The maximum is at most x exactly when all n observations are, and independence makes that a product of n identical factors. Option B is the cdf of the MINIMUM, and option A is the density of the maximum rather than its cdf.

items.stem: For a sample of size 4 from U(0, 1), E(X₍₂₎) is:
items.explanation: E(X₍ᵣ₎) = r/(n+1) = 2/5 = 0.4. Equivalently Beta(2, 3) has mean 2/(2+3). The four order statistics have means 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 — equally spaced at 1/(n+1) = 0.2.
items.check: The denominator is n + 1 = 5, not n = 4. Option C uses n and is the standard slip.

items.stem: For a sample of size 5 from U(0, 1), E(X₍₅₎) is:
items.explanation: The maximum is r = n = 5, so E = 5/(5+1) = 5/6 ≈ 0.8333. Checking independently, the maximum's density is 5x⁴ on (0,1), whose mean is ∫5x⁵dx = 5/6. The maximum's mean approaches 1 as n grows but never reaches it.
items.check: The expected maximum must be below 1 and above 1/2, which rules out options B and D at once.

items.stem: For a population with pdf f(x) = e^(−x), x ≥ 0, the cdf of X₍₇₎ in a sample of size 7 is:
items.explanation: The population cdf is F(x) = 1 − e^(−x), and the largest order statistic has cdf [F(x)]ⁿ, so (1 − e^(−x))⁷. Option B is the cdf of the MINIMUM of the seven, which is exponential with mean 1/7, and option A is a density, not a cdf.

items.stem: For a sample of size n from an exponential population with mean θ, X₍₁₎ has mean:
items.explanation: P(X₍₁₎ > x) = [1 − F(x)]ⁿ = (e^(−x/θ))ⁿ = e^(−nx/θ), which is the survival function of an exponential with mean θ/n. So the minimum of n exponentials is exponential again with the rate multiplied by n — a consequence of the memoryless property, and why a series system of many components fails early.

items.stem: For a sample from any distribution symmetric about μ, the sample median has expectation:
options: the population mean only if the population is normal
items.explanation: Symmetry pairs X₍ᵣ₎ with X₍ₙ₋ᵣ₊₁₎ as mirror images about μ, so E(X₍ᵣ₎) + E(X₍ₙ₋ᵣ₊₁₎) = 2μ. For odd n the median is its own mirror image, and for even n it is the average of a mirror pair — so the result holds either way, exactly, at every n. This is why the sample median is the standard robust estimator of location.

items.stem: The expected value of the sample range from U(0, 1) with n observations is:
items.explanation: E(R) = E(X₍ₙ₎) − E(X₍₁₎) = n/(n+1) − 1/(n+1) = (n−1)/(n+1). The subtraction needs only linearity of expectation, so the dependence between the minimum and the maximum is irrelevant here — though it would matter for Var(R).
items.check: At n = 2 this gives 1/3, which is the known mean absolute difference of two uniforms; at n = 20 it gives 0.905.

items.stem: The joint density of all n order statistics from a continuous population with density f is:
options: n! f(x₁)⋯f(xₙ) for x₁ < ⋯ < xₙ, zero otherwise
items.explanation: The n! counts the orderings of the original labelled sample that sort to the same vector, and the density is zero outside the increasing region. Option B would make the order statistics independent, which they never are — sorting forces X₍₁₎ ≤ X₍₂₎ ≤ ⋯, so their marginal densities must never be multiplied.

items.stem: For a sample of size 3 from U(0, 1), the variance of the median is:
items.explanation: The median of three is X₍₂₎ ~ Beta(2, 2). Var = r(n−r+1)/((n+1)²(n+2)) = 2×2/(16 × 5) = 4/80 = 1/20 = 0.05. The Beta formula ab/((a+b)²(a+b+1)) = 4/(16 × 5) agrees, which is a useful cross-check.
items.check: sd = √0.05 ≈ 0.224, about a quarter of the whole interval — a reminder of how little three observations pin down.

items.stem: Consider order statistics X₍₁₎ ≤ ⋯ ≤ X₍ₙ₎ from an independent continuous sample.
items.explanation: A is true, the defining product for the maximum. B is false — the order statistics are never independent, since sorting forces the ordering. C is true: expectation is linear, so no independence is needed for the mean of a difference. D is false: the cdf of the minimum is 1 − [1 − F]ⁿ, not 1 − Fⁿ.
statements: E(X₍ₙ₎ − X₍₁₎) = E(X₍ₙ₎) − E(X₍₁₎) regardless of their dependence.

A.why: True. The maximum is at most x exactly when all n observations are, and independence of the sample makes that a product.

B.why: False. Order statistics are never independent: X₍₁₎ ≤ X₍ₙ₎ always holds, which no pair of independent continuous variables satisfies.

C.why: True. Expectation is linear, so the mean of a difference is the difference of the means whatever the dependence. Only the VARIANCE of the range needs the covariance.

D.why: False. That expression is P(not all observations exceed x), a different event. The minimum's cdf is 1 − [1 − F(x)]ⁿ.

items.stem: Ten independent components each have exponential lifetime with mean 500 hours. The expected time to the FIRST failure is:
items.explanation: The minimum of n exponentials with mean θ is exponential with mean θ/n = 500/10 = 50 hours. Option D is the expected time to the LAST failure, θH₁₀ = 500 × 2.9290 = 1464 hours — so a series system of these components averages 50 hours while a parallel one lasts nearly thirty times as long.
items.check: The first of ten failures must come well before the mean life of one component, so any answer at or above 500 is wrong by inspection.

items.stem: For a sample of size 5 from U(0, 1), which order statistic has the LARGEST variance?
options: all five have the same variance
items.explanation: Var(X₍ᵣ₎) = r(6−r)/252, which is maximised at r = 3: 0.0357 for the median against 0.0198 at either end. The boundaries at 0 and 1 pin the extremes down while the middle is free to move. For a population with unbounded tails, such as the normal, the ordering reverses — so it is the population's shape that decides, not a general rule about extremes.

items.stem: The general density of X₍ᵣ₎ is f₍ᵣ₎(x) = C · [F(x)]^(r−1) [1 − F(x)]^(n−r) f(x). The constant C is:
items.explanation: Read it as a multinomial count: r − 1 observations fall below x, one sits at x, and n − r fall above, so C = n!/((r−1)! · 1! · (n−r)!). There is no factor for the single observation at x because 1! = 1. For U(0,1) this constant is exactly 1/B(r, n−r+1); at n = 5, r = 3 it is 30.

items.stem: For U(0, θ), the maximum X₍ₙ₎ is the maximum likelihood estimator of θ. Its expectation is:
items.explanation: Scaling: if U ~ U(0,1) then θU ~ U(0,θ), so E(X₍ₙ₎) = θ · n/(n+1). The MLE is therefore biased downwards — necessarily so, since the maximum of a sample can never exceed θ — and (n+1)X₍ₙ₎/n is the unbiased version, which is option A.
items.check: The estimate can never exceed θ, so its expectation must be strictly below θ — which rules out θ itself and (n+1)θ/n at once, leaving only a value below θ.

items.stem: Consider the probability integral transform and its consequences for order statistics.
items.explanation: A is true and is the transform itself. B is true because F is non-decreasing, so sorting is preserved. C is true, and it is why distribution-free quantile intervals exist. D is false — expectation does not pass through a non-linear function, so E(X₍ᵣ₎) is not F⁻¹ of the Beta mean in general.
statements: If X is continuous with cdf F, then F(X) ~ Uniform(0, 1).
F(X₍ᵣ₎) = U₍ᵣ₎, so F(X₍ᵣ₎) ~ Beta(r, n − r + 1) for every continuous population.
The p-quantile of X₍ᵣ₎ equals F⁻¹ applied to the p-quantile of Beta(r, n − r + 1).
E(X₍ᵣ₎) = F⁻¹(r/(n + 1)) for every continuous population.

A.why: True. P(F(X) ≤ u) = P(X ≤ F⁻¹(u)) = F(F⁻¹(u)) = u, so F(X) is exactly standard uniform.

B.why: True. F is non-decreasing, so it preserves order and F(X₍ᵣ₎) is the rᵗʰ order statistic of the transformed uniform sample — which makes the Beta result general, not special to the uniform.

C.why: True. Quantiles DO pass through a monotone transformation, which is exactly why exact distribution-free confidence intervals for a population quantile can be built from the Beta or the binomial.

D.why: False. Quantiles survive a monotone transformation but expectations do not: E(g(X)) ≠ g(E(X)) for non-linear g. The formula would hold only if F⁻¹ were linear.

items.stem: For a unit exponential population, P(X₍₇₎ ≤ 2) in a sample of size 7 is approximately:
items.explanation: (1 − e^(−2))⁷ = (0.86466)⁷ = 0.3614. Option B is F(2) for a single observation, and option C is the same expression at x = 1. So even with seven observations, the largest exceeds 2 about 64% of the time — raising a value to the 7th power punishes it hard.
items.check: 0.86466⁷ must be well below 0.86466; a rough check is 0.865⁷ ≈ e^(7 ln 0.865) = e^(−1.017) ≈ 0.36.

items.stem: Why are the middle order statistics of a uniform sample more variable than the extremes, while for a normal sample the reverse holds?
options: because the normal's order statistics are independent while the uniform's are not
because the normal has a larger variance than the uniform
because the uniform is discrete at its endpoints
on the uniform scale the middle is always most variable, and moving to X stretches by 1/f, which is huge in the normal's tails
items.explanation: The probability integral transform puts every continuous population on the uniform scale, where Var(U₍ᵣ₎) = r(n−r+1)/((n+1)²(n+2)) is largest in the middle. Moving back to X stretches by dx/du = 1/f(x). For the uniform f = 1 everywhere so the pattern survives; for the normal f is tiny in the tails, so the stretching there overwhelms it. The same factor 1/f appears in the large-sample variance of a sample quantile.

items.stem: A dam is designed using the largest annual flood in 80 years of record. The probability that a single new year exceeds that record is:
options: 1/2, since the record is the median
it cannot be found without knowing the flood distribution
items.explanation: Among 81 independent and identically distributed years, every ordering is equally likely, so each year is equally likely to be the largest; the chance the new one takes the record is 1/81. The argument uses only symmetry among exchangeable years, which is why option D is wrong — no distributional knowledge is needed. Over thirty years such exceedances are not remote, which is why a record is not a design ceiling.
